title: Case study: web crawler

kcs.statement: A crawler's URL frontier keeps a separate queue per host so that it fetches from each host one connection at a time with a delay. This politeness policy stops the crawler from overloading any one site.
Before a URL enters the frontier, the crawler normalises it and checks a seen-URL set, often a Bloom filter, so the same page is not crawled twice. A false positive only skips a page.
Different URLs often serve the same page. The crawler stores a content fingerprint (a hash of the page body) and drops pages whose fingerprint it has already seen.
A crawler fetches and caches robots.txt for each host and obeys it. It caps URL length and per-host depth to escape crawler traps such as infinite calendar pages.

problem_ideas: Crawl 1 billion pages a month at 100 KB each. Estimate pages per second and storage per month.
Design the frontier so that 1,000 workers never hit the same host concurrently.
A site generates /calendar?day=N for every N. Show how the crawler avoids crawling forever.
http://Example.com/a/../b and http://example.com/b: normalise both and dedupe them.
Explain why DNS resolution becomes a bottleneck at 10K fetches/s and how caching fixes it.
Prioritise news sites to be recrawled hourly and static sites monthly in one frontier.
